_note: Definitions for the term pages (brand / era / nib / filling mechanism), category intros and blog category descriptions. Every sentence traces to his posts (slugs named), his pages, or the catalog; facts with outside sources are in research/domain-facts.md.

01-pre-1900.definition: Before 1900 a fountain pen was an eyedropper: you unscrewed the section and poured ink straight into the hollow barrel. As he puts it in his Conklin post, "Before that you had dips and eyedroppers." Conklin's crescent filler of 1898 was one of the first self-fillers. Pens from this era are hard rubber, brittle with age, and old ink "effectively turns into glue" in their threads (when-hard-rubber-misbehaves).

02-1900-1919.definition: The first self-filling pens: crescent fillers, early lever fillers (Sheaffer's lever was patented in 1908), safeties and eyedroppers, almost all in black or mottled hard rubber. The flexible gold nibs collectors chase come mostly from these years. He restores hard rubber last: "most of these pens are made from black hard rubber more than 100 years ago, and they are very brittle" (how-do-i-restore-a-conklin-crescent).

03-1920-1929.definition: The Roaring Twenties: Parker's Duofold "Big Red" (1921), Sheaffer's Lifetime white dot (1924) and Balance (1929), Waterman's ripple hard rubber, Wahl-Eversharp's Gold Seal (1928). Colour arrives as celluloid replaces hard rubber, and button and lever fillers dominate. His rule for the decade's prices: "Big Reds are pretty common"; Mandarin Yellow is rare because "the material used to make the yellow turns very brittle with age" (how-do-i-start-collecting-pens-why-are-some-pens-more-than-others).

04-1930-1939.definition: Art deco and laminated celluloid. Parker introduced the Vacumatic in 1933; "Parker Vacumatics are my favorite. I love their stunning art deco designs and over-complicated filling system" (how-do-i-restore-a-parker-vacumatic). Sheaffer streamlined the Balance, Waterman made the Patrician and the Ink-Vue, Wahl the Doric. He calls the 1920s through the 1950s "really sort of the golden age of fountain pens" (The Day, 2022).

05-1940-1949.definition: Wartime and after: the Parker 51 (1941) with its hooded nib, Vacumatic-filling Duofolds he calls DuoVacs, Sheaffer's Triumph nib (1942), the Esterbrook J (1941), Eversharp's Skyline, and Parker's aerometric filler (1948). Gold trim thins while metal goes to the war. "If you get into vintage pen collecting, odds are really good that you'll encounter numerous 'Vacs' that need repair" (how-do-i-restore-a-parker-vacumatic).

06-1950-1959.definition: Sheaffer's pneumatic decade: TouchDown (1949), Snorkel (1952) and the PFM, "a luxury fountain pen first released in 1959" that "wasn't quite as popular in its time as it should have been" (shopping-for-a-sheaffer-pfm). Parker 51 aerometrics and the 61's capillary filler (1956), Montblanc's 1950s Meisterstücks and 6xx tier, Waterman's C/F cartridge pen (1953). The last decade before the ballpoint took over.

07-1960-1979.definition: Cartridge and converter filling becomes the norm: Parker 45 and 75, Sheaffer's inlaid nibs, Montblanc's modern 146 and 149 shape, Pelikan's revised piston fillers, and a great many ballpoints and pencils. Many of the pre-owned bargains in the case come from these years, and most are simple to keep running.

08-1980-present.definition: Modern pens, bought pre-owned: Montblanc, Pelikan's M800 (1987), Namiki maki-e, Visconti, Delta, Omas, Aurora, Lamy, TWSBI. Most fill by cartridge/converter or piston. His advice: "there is a great deal of money to be saved by purchasing luxury pens from Cross to Montblanc on the second-hand market," and to check the dealer first: "Is there a return policy? Do the descriptions honestly address damage and wear on the pens?" (how-do-i-start-collecting-pens-vintage-vs-modern).

accountant.definition: Sheaffer's "A" point: thinner than an extra-fine, made for ledgers and small figures. His nib guide notes that in the 1950s Sheaffer used a letter for the point (A, B, F, G, M, S, X) and a digit for the material (a-nib-by-any-other-numberis-still-confusing). Four in the catalog carry it.

extra-fine.definition: "XF = Extra Fine" in his nib-search key (search-by-nib-size): a Western extra-fine lays down a line around 0.3 mm, roughly what a Japanese maker calls a fine. Good for small handwriting and cheap paper; the least forgiving of dry ink.

fine.definition: "F = Fine": about 0.4 to 0.5 mm, the everyday width and the most common nib in the case. He reads them honestly: "Marked 'F' for fine, we think it is a really generous fine. We would call it a medium" (SKU 6960). Watch for what he calls tweener pens, "a fine-medium or a medium-broad, that sort of thing" (search-by-nib-size).

medium.definition: "M = Medium": about 0.6 to 0.7 mm, the all-rounder that shows ink colour without demanding good paper. Nearly as common in the catalog as fine. His descriptions say how wet or dry each one writes, because a medium from 1935 and a medium from 1995 are not the same line.

broad1.definition: "B = Broad": about 0.8 to 1.0 mm, wet and bold, the width that lets shading inks shade. Rare in vintage American pens, where fine sold best; look for them on 1950s Sheaffers and modern European pens.

bb1.definition: "BB = Double Broad": 1.0 to 1.2 mm, a line for signatures and for inks you want to see. The catalog rarely has more than one at a time.

stub.definition: "Stub = Awesomeness" in his key (search-by-nib-size). A stub is cut flat and rounded, so downstrokes are wide and cross strokes thin; an italic is the crisp version. Esterbrook's 9314F "wrote a fine stub line for a fancy writing effect or calligraphy" (esterbrook-nibs-its-time-for-a-change). Lamy's calligraphy nibs run 1.1 to 1.9 mm.

oblique.definition: "O = Oblique": the tip is cut at an angle for writers who hold the pen rotated. Sheaffer marked left and right obliques with an L or R suffix, and the number on a vintage nib rarely tells you what it is: "it is really difficult to gauge a nib by its number" (a-nib-by-any-other-numberis-still-confusing).

semi-flexible.definition: "SF = Semi-Flex": the tines spread with moderate pressure and the line widens, without the wet-noodle feel of a true flex. Many 1920s and 1930s gold nibs in the case are semi-flexible; the Montblanc 644's "semi-flexible two-tone 14k gold nib" "starts as a medium and can be gently worked into a wide line" (SKU 6967).

flexible.definition: "FLEXI = Flexible, somewhere in the vicinity of wet noodle" (search-by-nib-size). Light pressure takes the line from hairline to a swell, the vintage magic that modern steel cannot copy. Rare and priced accordingly: he uses the Waterman 52 as the example of a flex pen collectors pay for (how-do-i-start-collecting-pens-why-are-some-pens-more-than-others).

lever-filler.definition: The lever on the barrel presses a bar against a rubber sac; release it and the sac draws ink. Sheaffer patented it in 1908 and most American pens from the 1910s to the 1950s use it. The sac hardens with age and needs replacing: a resac, the repair he does most. On his repair list.

button-filler.definition: Unscrew the blind cap, press the button, and a spring bar flexes the sac; Parker's Duofold made it famous in the 1920s. Restoration is a new sac plus a check of the pressure bar. On his repair list ("Button Fillers").

vacumatic.definition: Parker's sac-less system of 1933: a plunger flexes a rubber diaphragm and the barrel itself holds the ink, so the laminated celluloid shows the level. "Restoring these pens is both easy and complicated. It really just depends on how lucky you get," and it takes a special Vac unit tool; "for the love of all that you hold dear, keep celluloid pens away from open flames" (how-do-i-restore-a-parker-vacumatic). On his repair list.

snorkel.definition: Sheaffer's 1952 answer to inky fingers: a tube extends from under the nib, and a pneumatic stroke of the blind cap collapses the sac and fills the pen without dipping the nib. The PFM of 1959 used a larger version. Repair means sac, O-ring and point seal; the PFM needs "a special tool" (shopping-for-a-sheaffer-pfm). On his repair list.

touchdown.definition: Sheaffer's pneumatic filler of 1949: pull the blind cap, push it down, and air pressure collapses the sac, which then draws ink. "Fixing a Sheaffer TouchDown filler can be easy with a little practice. Personally, I love the functionality and simplicity of the design" (how-do-i-restore-a-sheaffer-touchdown). Repair is a new sac and O-ring. On his repair list.

aerometric-filler.definition: Parker's 1948 squeeze filler for the 51: a pli-glass sac inside a metal sleeve with a breather tube, pressed a few times to fill. The sacs rarely fail, which is why aerometric 51s are the daily drivers he recommends; when they do, it is a clean and a resac. On his repair list ("Aerometrics").

crescent-filler.definition: "Conklin invented the crescent filler in 1898. For as cumbersome as it looks, it was an insanely simple design": a crescent through the barrel presses the sac, and a lock ring keeps it from filling in your pocket (how-do-i-restore-a-conklin-crescent). Mark Twain endorsed it. Hard rubber and old, so he soaks briefly and heats gently. On his repair list.

eyedropper.definition: The oldest system: the barrel is the reservoir and you fill it with a dropper. Old ink glues the section threads, so "fill a cup with room-temperature water and soak the pen over the line separating the section from the barrel. Let it soak for 12 to 48 hours" (when-hard-rubber-misbehaves). Modern Ranga pens in the catalog are eyedroppers by design.

safety.definition: An eyedropper whose nib retracts into the barrel by a twist of the tail so the cap can seal it, hence the name. Early 1900s Waterman and Montblanc made them; the packing seal is what fails. Outside his published repair scope.

bulb-postal-filler.definition: A rubber bulb in place of a blind cap; squeeze it a few times and the sac fills. A 1920s and 1930s system used by makers such as Chilton and Sheaffer's postal pens. Restoration is a new bulb and sac.

vacuum-fil.definition: Sheaffer's plunger filler of the 1930s and 1940s (also Onoto's): one stroke of the plunger creates a vacuum that fills the whole barrel. The packing seal is the failure point. He no longer restores "Sheaffer piston fillers" (pen-repairs page), so these are sold restored but not taken in for repair.

capillary.definition: Parker's 61 (1956) fills by capillary action: dip the tail and a cell of folded plastic draws ink with no moving parts. It clogs when neglected and is close to unrepairable, which is why a working 61 is described carefully. Outside his repair list.

piston.definition: A knob at the tail drives a piston down the barrel; Pelikan made it standard in 1929 and Montblanc, Aurora and Omas followed. The Montblanc 644's telescoping piston "still works smoothly! Talk about remarkable German engineering" (SKU 6967). He no longer restores "European, Nozac and Sheaffer piston fillers" (pen-repairs page).

cartridge-converter.definition: Waterman's C/F of 1953 started it: a disposable cartridge, or a converter that screws in and fills from a bottle. Nearly every pen made after 1960 uses it, and most of the pre-owned modern pens in the case do. Nothing to restore; the converter is a part, not a repair.

ballpoint.definition: Refill-fed pens with a rolling ball; here they are pre-owned Parker Jotters, Caran d'Ache, Montblanc and Cross ballpoints. Nothing to fill and nothing to resac. He notes when a standard refill fits.

rollerball.definition: A liquid-ink refill behind a rolling ball: the fountain pen's line without the nib. Pre-owned Pelikan, Montblanc and Waterman rollerballs sit in this group. Refills are standard sizes.

pencil.definition: Mechanical pencils from the same makers as the pens: Parker, Sheaffer, Wahl-Eversharp, Conklin. Twist or push mechanisms, mostly 1.1 mm leads on the vintage ones. He describes lead size and whether the mechanism advances cleanly.

dip.definition: A nib in a holder with no reservoir; you dip it. He sells the occasional dip pen and inkwell together, and his blog counts dip pens among the four kinds worth collecting (how-do-i-start-collecting-pens-know-thy-obsession).

syringe.definition: A rare 1930s system with a syringe-style plunger. Nothing in the catalog uses it today; the page exists because his old site listed the term.

parker.definition: Parker is the largest marque in the case, with the Duofold, Vacumatic and 51 from Janesville, Wisconsin. Vacumatics are his favourite vintage Parkers for their "stunning art deco designs and over-complicated filling system" (how-do-i-restore-a-parker-vacumatic); the Duofold "Big Red" is the pen he uses to explain why some pens cost more than others.

sheaffer.definition: Sheaffer of Fort Madison, Iowa: the lever filler (1908), the Lifetime white dot (1924), the Balance (1929), then the pneumatic TouchDown, Snorkel and PFM. His grandfather's Sheaffer Lifetime Balance was the pen that started him at age 9 (about-us). He restores every Sheaffer sac filler and has written bench guides for the TouchDown and the PFM.

waterman.definition: Waterman of New York, the flexible-nib house of the 1910s and 1920s: the 52, the Patrician, the Ink-Vue, then the C/F cartridge pen of 1953 and today's French-made Charleston and Carène. He uses the Waterman 52 as the example of a flex nib collectors pay for.

wahl-eversharp.definition: Wahl-Eversharp of Chicago: the Gold Seal pens (1928), the faceted Doric (1931) and the Skyline (1941), plus the mechanical pencils that gave the company its name. Several Gold Seals are usually in the case, some on sale.

conklin.definition: Conklin of Toledo, Ohio invented the crescent filler in 1898, the pen Mark Twain endorsed, and followed it with the Endura in 1924. His bench post on restoring a Conklin Crescent is the one to read before touching a hard rubber pen.

esterbrook.definition: Esterbrook of Camden, New Jersey made the J series (1941 on) with screw-in nib units, "dozens of different sizes and strengths for different jobs," so "all you had to do was unscrew the old nib and replace it with a new one" (esterbrook-nibs-its-time-for-a-change). His recommended first vintage pen: "Start safely with a few fully restored $50 Parkers, Sheaffers or even Esterbrooks."

mont-blanc.definition: Montblanc of Hamburg: the 1950s Meisterstücks (142, 144, 146, 149) and the 6xx tier, then the modern 146 and 149, Solitaires and limited editions, bought pre-owned. He has written ten posts on spotting fake Montblancs; every Montblanc here is described with its serial number and what he checked.

pelikan.definition: Pelikan of Hanover made the piston filler standard in 1929; the 400 of the 1950s and the M800 (1987) are the ones that come through the case. Like Esterbrook, Pelikan lets you swap nib units, which he calls the two makers that "made it easy to exchange nibs on one pen you already love."

namiki-pilot.definition: Pilot of Tokyo (1918) and its Namiki maki-e line: lacquer work by hand, sold pre-owned and complete with box when he has it. Japanese nibs run a grade finer than Western ones, which his descriptions note.

montegrappa.definition: Montegrappa of Bassano del Grappa, Italy, since 1912: celluloid and sterling pens, sold here pre-owned.

omas.definition: Omas of Bologna (1925): faceted celluloid pens with piston fillers, the Paragon and the Arte Italiana. Pre-owned examples appear a few at a time.

aurora.definition: Aurora of Turin (1919), Italy's oldest pen maker still in business: the 88 and the Optima, with their own gold nibs. Pre-owned.

visconti.definition: Visconti of Florence (1988): celluloid and resin pens with unusual filling systems. Pre-owned.

lamy.definition: Lamy of Heidelberg: the 2000, the Safari, and the left-handed steel nibs he found a trove of when a distributorship changed hands. His advice for a first pen mentions Lamy by name (how-do-i-start-collecting-pens-vintage-vs-modern).

twsbi.definition: TWSBI of Taiwan: piston-filling demonstrators such as the Eco and the 580, which he lists among the brands "to build up a daily-use collection on a budget."

cross.definition: A. T. Cross of Rhode Island, the oldest American maker: ballpoints, the Townsend and Century II fountain pens. He does not buy Cross Century pens (sell-my-pens page) but sells the occasional one pre-owned.

caran-dache.definition: Caran d'Ache of Geneva: lacquer and metal pens, "a rare and luxurious pen" when the Chinese Lacquer ballpoint came through (SKU 4610). Pre-owned.

s-t-dupont.definition: S.T. Dupont of Paris: lacquer-over-brass pens and lighters. Pre-owned.

delta.definition: Delta of Naples (1982): resin and celluloid pens including the Dolcevita. Pre-owned.

cartier.definition: Cartier pens, made under licence in the 1980s and 1990s. Pre-owned.

dunhill.definition: Dunhill of London, whose 1930 partnership with Namiki brought maki-e to the West. Pre-owned.

eagle.definition: Eagle Pencil Company of New York: inexpensive vintage pens and pencils of the 1920s and 1930s, often the least expensive fountain pens in the case.

franklin-christoph.definition: Franklin-Christoph of North Carolina: modern American pens with nib choices. Pre-owned.

sailor.definition: Sailor of Hiroshima (1911): the 1911 and Pro Gear with in-house gold nibs. Pre-owned.

stipula.definition: Stipula of Florence: celluloid pens, sold pre-owned.

taccia.definition: Taccia: modern pens with Japanese nibs and urushi finishes. Pre-owned.

bexley.definition: Bexley of Columbus, Ohio: modern American pens in vintage shapes. Pre-owned.

ranga.definition: Ranga of India: hand-turned ebonite eyedroppers and cartridge pens, often with flexible or semi-flexible nibs. Pre-owned.

laban.definition: Laban of Taiwan: resin pens with steel nibs. Pre-owned.

levenger.definition: Levenger: the True Writer line. Pre-owned.

leboeuf.definition: LeBoeuf of Springfield, Massachusetts: 1920s and 1930s celluloid pens with unbreakable barrels, scarce.

marlen.definition: Marlen of Italy: limited-edition resin pens. Pre-owned.

michel-perchin.definition: Michel Perchin: Fabergé-style enamel and vermeil pens made in the 1990s, the Imperial Russia editions. Pre-owned and among the grails.

jean-pierre-lepine.definition: Jean Pierre Lépine of France: sculptural modern pens. Pre-owned.

signum.definition: Signum of Italy: resin pens with gold nibs. Pre-owned.

faber-castell.definition: Faber-Castell of Stein, Germany, and its Graf von Faber-Castell line. Pre-owned.

diamond-medal.definition: Diamond Medal: a 1920s and 1930s second-tier American brand, the sort of pen his nib post lines up beside a Sheaffer to show that nib numbers never matched between makers.

epenco.definition: Epenco (Eagle Pencil Company): inexpensive 1930s pens and sets.

acme.definition: Acme Studio: designer rollerballs and ballpoints. Pre-owned.

carters.definition: Carter's Ink Company of Boston, better known for ink and the Inx inkwells that appear in the inkwells and blotters category; it also made pens briefly around 1930.

conway-stewart.definition: Conway Stewart of London: casein and celluloid lever fillers of the 1930s to 1950s, and the modern revival. Vintage and pre-owned.

other.definition: Makers with one or two pens in the case: unbranded and warranted-nib pens, small American and European houses, and the occasional camera, thermometer or inkwell that does not belong to a pen marque.

vintage-pens.intro: Restored vintage fountain pens from the 1890s to the 1970s, one of each. Every pen was disassembled, fitted with a new sac or seal where it takes one, tuned and test-written before it was listed, and each description ends with the capped length and the flaws stated plainly. Sold under the 14-day guarantee.
vintage-pens.meta_description: Restored vintage fountain pens: Parker, Sheaffer, Waterman, Wahl-Eversharp, Conklin and Esterbrook, tested and guaranteed by ThePenMarket.com. One of each.

pre-owned-pens.intro: Pre-owned modern pens from Montblanc, Pelikan, Namiki, Omas, Aurora, Visconti, Lamy and others, mostly 1980 to now. Bought second-hand "there is a great deal of money to be saved" (his words), and each listing says what was checked, what came with it and how the nib writes.
pre-owned-pens.meta_description: Pre-owned luxury fountain pens, rollerballs and ballpoints from Montblanc, Pelikan, Namiki and more, described honestly and guaranteed by ThePenMarket.com.

pencils.intro: Mechanical pencils from the same makers as the pens: Parker, Sheaffer, Wahl-Eversharp and Conklin among them. Twist and push mechanisms, mostly 1.1 mm leads on the vintage pieces, described with lead size and whether the mechanism advances cleanly.
pencils.meta_description: Vintage mechanical pencils by Parker, Sheaffer, Wahl-Eversharp and Conklin, working and described honestly, from ThePenMarket.com.

inkwells-blotters.intro: Inkwells, rocker blotters and desk pieces from the fountain pen's own era: Carter's Inx glass, cast-metal desk sets and the like. The small collection that keeps a desk honest.
inkwells-blotters.meta_description: Vintage inkwells and rocker blotters, including Carter's Inx glass, from ThePenMarket.com.

camera.intro: A few vintage cameras, new to the site in 2025 and described the way the pens are: what works, what shows wear, and what it comes with.
camera.meta_description: Vintage cameras, described and guaranteed like the pens, from ThePenMarket.com.

memberships.intro: The Unlimited Posts membership for the Trading Post: "Upload as many writing instruments and related ephemera as you want for one calendar year starting from the day you purchase this membership."
memberships.meta_description: Unlimited Posts: one year of unlimited Trading Post listings on ThePenMarket.com for $125.

pen-news.definition: Shop news, pen show reports (Chicago, DC, Dallas and Ohio through 2020), holiday shipping deadlines and what came in this month. The running diary of ThePenMarket.com since 2013.

original-stories.definition: Fiction and essays written here: the Decameron 2020 project, the Westenra Memorial stave, the ninth-anniversary novel post. The writer behind the repairman.

famous-people-pens.definition: The pens of presidents, writers and spies: Truman's bill-signing pens, Eisenhower's Parker 51, Mark Twain's Conklin Crescent, James Bond's Montblanc. Thirty-one posts on who wrote with what.

ink-reviews.definition: Inks under the sun and the pH meter: the UV fade tests that leave bottles on a windowsill for a year, the pH readings that explain why some inks eat sacs, and which inks are safe in a vintage pen. Twenty-nine posts, the sunburned-inks series among them.

notes-from-the-work-bench.definition: How the restorations are done: re-saccing a lever filler, restoring a Parker Vacumatic, a Sheaffer TouchDown, a Conklin Crescent, polishing celluloid by wet sanding, and the snorkels that fought back. The bench posts new collectors are sent to first.

how-do-i-start-collecting-pens.definition: The seventeen-post series for new collectors: know thy obsession, vintage versus modern, why some pens cost more than others, investing, fake Montblanc serial numbers, and how to buy safely from a dealer.

pen-ads-of-yesteryear.definition: Vintage pen advertisements read closely: what Parker, Sheaffer and Eversharp promised in the 1920s to 1950s, and what the pens actually did.

pens-writing.definition: Handwriting, thank-you notes, cursive's history and why modern books are not called classics: the writing side of the writing instrument.

the-history-of-pens.definition: Where the pens came from: the companies, the patents and the materials, from hard rubber to celluloid to the ballpoint.

book-reviews.definition: Books about pens and pen makers, reviewed: Waterman past and present, a hundred years of Sheaffer, and the like.

uncategorized-new.definition: Posts that did not get a category on the old site.
